summary: Mount Chase, Penobscot Co., ME: wooden tower 1909, 16-ft steel tower 1917; steel tower moved in 2001 to Patten Lumbermen's Museum; summit has a radio tower, no fire tower.

facts.design: 16-ft steel tower erected 1917 to replace a wooden tower of 1909 (1917 annual report; 1920 inventory says 12 ft)
facts.status_note: Tower taken down in 2001 and moved to the Patten Lumbermen's Museum; the summit now has a communications building and a radio tower, not a fire tower

access.note: Reached by a hiking trail to the summit; the sources describe no closure and do not name the landowner

visit.trail_note: Side trail of about 1.7 miles that starts where Mountain Road meets the Shin Pond ATV Trail

events.note: First fire tower on Mount Chase was a wooden structure (photo inventory, Maine Historical Society)
One-room watchman's cabin built below the summit; used until 1922
1912 Forest Commissioner's report: station in good condition

Letter of November 15, 1916 from chief warden Leon C. Irish, relaying advice from Mr. Murphy ('the United States man'): a floor and windows should be placed in the lookout house; also recommended moving the house a little northwest
Wooden tower replaced by a 16-foot steel tower (1917 Annual Report of the Forest Commissioner)
Inventory indicates a 12-foot steel tower; conflicts with the 16 feet recorded in 1917
Second, larger watchman's cabin replaced the first
Steel tower taken down and moved to the Patten Lumbermen's Museum

corrections.why: The FFLOS register and the Maine IAT post both date the move to 2001; the record leaves the year blank

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The 1917 annual report and the 1HappyHiker blog give 16 feet; the 1920 inventory gives 12 feet. facts use the 1917 figure (4.9 m) and the 1920 figure is kept as an assessed event
A 2018 blog post describes the cabin interior as dilapidated; a later hike report says most of the cabin is still standing. Both are reported; the sources do not say when its condition changed
The FFLOS register, the Maine IAT post and the 1HappyHiker blog all give 2001 for the move, so no conflict

notes_for_editor: The summit has no fire tower but does have a communications building and radio tower, per the 2018 and 2021 accounts; both are blog or hike reports, not agency records. The 1917 height (16 ft) and the 1920 inventory (12 ft) disagree. The museum home page lists admission rates ($12 ages 12-65, $10 ages 65+, $7 ages 4-12) and does not mention the tower; whether the tower display is covered by admission was not confirmed. The sister record us-me-chase-mountain-tower-site-at-patten-lumbermens-museum is the moved tower. No new photos found.
